definition: In the field of computer vision, any two images of the same planar surface in space are related by a homography (assuming a pinhole camera model).
details: This has many practical applications, such as image rectification, image registration, or camera motion—rotation and translation—between two images. Once camera resectioning has been done from an estimated homography matrix, this information may be used for navigation, or to insert models of 3D objects into an image or video, so that they are rendered with the correct perspective and appear to have been part of the original scene (see Augmented reality).

explainer.lead: In computer vision, any two images of the same planar surface are related by a homography, assuming a pinhole camera model. It matters because it lets systems map points between views for rectification, registration, and inserting 3D objects with correct perspective.

tiers.eli5: If you photograph a flat poster from two angles, a homography is the rule that tells you where each point on the poster lands in the other photo.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers estimate a homography matrix to rectify or register images, or to infer camera rotation and translation between two views. A pitfall is that the mapping assumes a planar surface and a pinhole camera model, so it breaks when that fails.
tiers.paperLevel: Points on a plane in two views are related by a 3x3 homography matrix under the pinhole model; once camera resectioning is done from it, the result supports navigation or 3D object insertion. Its validity depends on the planar-surface and pinhole assumptions.

explainer.example: After estimating the homography between two photos of a wall, a system inserts a rendered 3D model into the second photo with the correct perspective so it looks part of the scene.
